chapter_theme: Madhavi's debut: after seven years of training she is presented to the Chola king with a troupe each of whose masters is described by his art, on a stage built to the treatise's measures; the talaikkol, a war trophy worshipped as Indra's son, is carried round the town, she dances, wins the title and 1008 kazhanju, and her garland, priced at that sum and offered in the street, is bought by Kovalan, who goes to live with her and forgets his home.

cast.role: the dancer of Puhar, of a line traced to the heavenly women freed from a curse
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the unnamed Chola king of Puhar, here சூழ்கடல் மன்னன், காவல் வேந்தன்
the poet of the troupe, master of Tamil and the drama treatise
the master of the thannumai drum
the yaazh player who tunes the modes
the senior dancing women who sing the opening vaaram
the doe-eyed woman, unnamed here, who calls Madhavi 'our creeper' and sends her garland out for sale
the hunchbacked maid who carries the garland into the street

silappathikaram:3:1-11.reading: Madhavi, of a birth not falling short of the heavenly women freed at the place of the talaikkol from the curse a holy sage of the divine mountain laid on them with Indra's son, trains seven years in dance, song and beauty, lacking in none of the three, to show her art to the sea-girt king in her twelfth year.
silappathikaram:3:1-11.nuance: The sage gives the curse 'as grace' (அருள எய்திய சாபத்து), so the curse is framed as a gift. Whether Madhavi descends from the freed heavenly women or only matches them (பிறப்பிற் குன்றா, a birth not less than theirs) cannot be fixed from these lines; the sage and the heavenly woman are not named. The three arts are counted as a set that must be whole (ஒன்றுகுறை படாமல்), so beauty stands among the trained skills, not as a gift of nature.
silappathikaram:3:1-11.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the first unit ends at line 11 (காட்டல் வேண்டி), where the account of Madhavi's training gives way to the dance master; the old unit 1-16 ran five lines into his description.
silappathikaram:3:1-11.event: Madhavi trains seven years in dance, song and beauty to be shown to the Chola king in her twelfth year.

silappathikaram:3:12-25.reading: The dance master is described: he knows the marks of the two kinds of koothu, joins the many kinds to the interludes, knows the eleven dances with their song and drumming, the four kinds of hand gesture and how a gesture of one style is dropped into another, and directs the kuravai and vari without mixing them.
silappathikaram:3:12-25.nuance: The four lines 20 to 23 are built as a chiasmus (கூடை into வாரம், வாரம் into கூடை, பிண்டி into ஆடல், ஆடல் into பிண்டி): the verse performs the exchange of gestures it describes. The master is praised for knowing where each gesture must stop, not for invention.
silappathikaram:3:12-25.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 12 (இருவகைக் கூத்தின்) to line 25, which closes the dance master's description with ஆசான் தன்னொடும்.

silappathikaram:3:26-36.reading: The singer is described: he fits the song to yaazh, flute, beat, voice and drum, keeps to the sound of the regional styles and knows them all without fault, and when the poem's intent, the dance and the parts of the song are set together, lays out his flawless learning.
silappathikaram:3:26-36.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 26 (யாழும் குழலும்) to line 36, which names the singer (இசையோன் தானும்) and closes his description.

silappathikaram:3:37-44.reading: The poet is described: knowing all of Tamil so that the Tamil land within the sea knows it, holding to the drama treatise in its two kinds, the king's style and the common style, he understands where the singer bends the melody and sets it in the fixed tradition, and knows the faults that rivals charge.
silappathikaram:3:37-44.nuance: The poet's office is partly defensive: he must know the blame (வசைமொழி) that others will speak, so the performance is judged against a rule that critics also hold. The pair வேத்தியல் பொதுவியல் recurs in the Manimekalai's list of Madhavi's arts.
silappathikaram:3:37-44.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 37 (இமிழ்கடல் வரைப்பில்) to line 44, which names the poet (நன்னூல் புலவனும்).

silappathikaram:3:45-55.reading: The drum master is described: knowing dance, song, melody, Tamil, mode, beat, rhythm, the lame measure and the regional styles, he lets the yaazh, flute and voice be heard in the measures of the dance, strikes the stroke at its sign, and swells or restrains it so that it never overpowers.
silappathikaram:3:45-55.nuance: The drummer's excellence is restraint: ஆக்கலும் அடக்கலும் மீத்திறம் படாமை, raising and holding back without excess. The loudest instrument is praised for not drowning the others.
silappathikaram:3:45-55.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 45 (ஆடல் பாடல் இசையே) to line 55, which names the drum master (தண்ணுமை அருந்தொழில் முதல்வனும்).

silappathikaram:3:56-69.reading: The flute player is described: knowing the fixed figures and the four ornaments, hearing the two strings kural and ili as one, keeping in step with the drum master and the tuned yaazh, he follows the singer's melody, carries on what has come and anticipates what comes, and plays each syllable on the wet stops without fault.
silappathikaram:3:56-69.nuance: The terms of art (சித்திர வஞ்சனை, வர்த்தனை, ஈர நிலம்) are not explained in the verse, and their exact sense is a reading I cannot fix without commentary.
silappathikaram:3:56-69.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 56 (சொல்லிய இயல்பினிற்) to line 69, which names the flute player (குழலோன் தானும்).

silappathikaram:3:70-94.reading: The yaazh player is described: to fix the seven palai modes from the fourteen strings, he moves notes by their kin, the high and low parts of the scale passing to one another until the red palai, then the other palais, are set, and he matches the yaazh and flute so that strong, soft and level are all in tune.
silappathikaram:3:70-94.nuance: The notes are treated as women who leave or join their kin (கிளைவழிப் பட்டனள், ஏனை மகளிரும் கிளைவழிச் சேர): the modal shift is told as a family moving house. The technical sequence (படுமலை, செவ்வழி, கோடி விளரி) is the verse's own, but which note becomes the tonic at each step is beyond what I can fix.
silappathikaram:3:70-94.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 70 (ஈர்ஏழ் தொடுத்த) to line 94, which names the yaazh player (புலமை யோனுடன்) and ends the list of accompanists.

silappathikaram:3:95-110.reading: The stage is built as the treatise's authors prescribe: on chosen ground, with a bamboo from the holy mountain whose internodes are a span apart, a measuring rod of twenty-four finger-breadths fixes it seven rods wide, eight long and one high, four rods between the planks, two doors, the guardian beings painted above and worshipped, lamps set so no pillar casts a shadow, and three kinds of curtain.
silappathikaram:3:95-110.nuance: Every measure is given as a number from the book (நூல்நெறி மரபின்), and the rod itself is taken from a holy mountain: the stage is a ritual space before it is a theatre. The lamps are placed so the pillars' shadows fall outside, so nothing on the stage is hidden.
silappathikaram:3:95-110.event: The stage is measured and built by rule, with painted guardians, lamps and three curtains.

silappathikaram:3:111-128.reading: Pearl garlands are hung from the painted canopy; the talaikkol, cut from the shaft of a white umbrella taken from great kings who fled, its joints set with nine gems and bound in gold, is worshipped in the king's palace as Jayanta son of Indra, bathed from a golden pot, garlanded, set in the state elephant's hand on an auspicious day, and carried round the town by the king and the five great assemblies to be set before the stage.
silappathikaram:3:111-128.nuance: The dancer's staff of honour is a war trophy: the shaft of a defeated king's umbrella. The emblem of an art is made from the emblem of a lost kingdom, and worshipped as a god, so the dance's highest title carries the Chola's victory and the Indra myth at once. What கவிகைக் கொடுப்ப (line 127) gives, and to whom, is unclear to me.
silappathikaram:3:111-128.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 111 (ஓவிய விதானத்து) to line 128, where the procession ends with புகுந்துமுன் வைத்துஆங்கு; the old unit stopped at 126 in mid-procession.
silappathikaram:3:111-128.event: The talaikkol, worshipped as Jayanta, is bathed, garlanded and carried on the state elephant round the town by the king and the five great assemblies, then set before the stage.

silappathikaram:3:129-153.reading: The musicians take their places by order; the dancer steps onto the stage right foot first and goes to the right pillar as custom requires, while the senior dancing women at the left pillar sing the two vaaram for good fortune and to keep off harm; the instruments follow one another, yaazh after flute, drum after yaazh, muzhavu after drum, the aamanthirikai with them, through eleven rounds, and then the dance begins on the palai mode in its counted measures.
silappathikaram:3:129-153.nuance: Madhavi is not named here; she is known from the right-foot entry, a rule of conduct (வழக்குஎனப் பொருந்தி). The order of the instruments is itself a hierarchy, each standing 'behind' (வழி) the one before. The counted measures of lines 148 to 153 are technical and I read only their outline.
silappathikaram:3:129-153.unit_note: Boundaries moved: the unit runs from line 129 (இயல்பினின் வழாஅ) to line 153, where the opening rounds end with மயங்கிய பின்றை; the old units 127-137 and 138-153 split the entry from the music it opens.
silappathikaram:3:129-153.event: Madhavi enters the stage right foot first, the senior dancers sing the two vaaram, the orchestra plays in its order, and the dance begins.

silappathikaram:3:154-175.reading: Having shown the dance as the treatise prescribes, Madhavi receives from the king the leaf garland and the talaikkol title and, by rule, a thousand and eight kazhanju of gold; the doe-eyed woman sets that sum as the price of the garland and sends it by a hunchbacked maid into the street of the town's young men as if for sale; Kovalan buys it, enters the bridal house with Madhavi, and in his union with her, infatuated and knowing no letting go, forgets his own house of flawless distinction.
silappathikaram:3:154-175.nuance: The garland's price is exactly the king's reward, so the courtesan house turns a royal honour into a sale price. The sale is staged (பகர்வனர் போல்வதோர் பான்மையின், 'in the manner of those who sell'): the street offer is a custom, not a bargain. The narrator passes no verdict on Madhavi; his one judgment is the praise of what Kovalan forgot (வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின்தன் மனையகம்), and the forgetting is told as infatuation (மயங்கி, விடுதல் அறியா விருப்பினன்), not as fate. Who the doe-eyed woman is, Madhavi's mother or another of the house, the chapter does not say.
silappathikaram:3:154-175.event: The king gives Madhavi the talaikkol and 1008 kazhanju; her garland, priced at that sum, is offered in the street, and Kovalan buys it, goes to live with Madhavi and forgets his home.

silappathikaram:3:176-179.reading: A closing venba says that Madhavi of Puhar, with her golden bangles, came onto the dancing stage and by her art displayed on earth the counts and letters, the five modes of composition, the four panns and the eleven dances set to music.
silappathikaram:3:176-179.nuance: The venba sums up the chapter as Madhavi's achievement and says nothing of the sale or of Kovalan: the closing praise and the narrative's last line (Kovalan forgetting his home) are set side by side without comment.

links.note: Madhavi's line is traced to heavenly women freed from a sage's curse, shared with Indra's son, at the place of the talaikkol; the talaikkol staff she later receives is worshipped as Jayanta, Indra's son.
links.teaches: The staff of honour Madhavi wins is the figure of the curse's release that her own descent goes back to, so her investiture re-enacts that release at the very moment she enters the bond that will undo Kovalan.

links.note: Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland at the price of the king's 1008 kazhanju and forgets his home; returning to Kannaki, he says that sporting with a deceiver (சலதி) has wasted the mountain of wealth his line gave him.
links.teaches: The narrator tells the purchase as a rule-bound custom and blames no one, and only later does Kovalan himself call Madhavi a deceiver and the purchase a ruin, so the epic lets the buyer, not the poet, put the blame on the seller.

links.note: The Silappathikaram tells Madhavi's seven years of training to be shown to the king; in the Manimekalai, Vasantamalai lists her arts item by item, opening with the same pair வேத்தியல் பொதுவியல், and reports the town saying her turn to tapas is shameful.
links.teaches: The accomplishment that the first epic crowns with the king's title becomes, in the sequel, the inventory of what Madhavi has given up, so the length of her training is what makes the town read her renunciation as a disgrace.

links.note: Kovalan, infatuated, knows no letting go (விடுதல் அறியா விருப்பினன்) once he buys the garland; in the Manimekalai, Madhavi tells how Aravana taught her that the great sorrow of the born comes from attachment (பற்றின் வருவது) and gave her the five precepts.
links.teaches: The sequel's Buddhist teaching names as attachment the cause that the first epic's narrator only shows as an infatuation that cannot let go, so the garland scene becomes the case the doctrine later diagnoses, told to the woman who sold the garland.

links.note: The couplet warns that the sweet words of bangled women who want wealth and not love bring harm; in the epic the garland priced at the king's reward is sent into the street by the doe-eyed woman, Madhavi speaks no word, and Kovalan buys it of his own infatuation.
links.teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single figure into a household that sets the price in the king's own coin and a dancer who is silent, so the harm the couplet lays on the woman's sweet speech here comes from a public custom and from the buyer's own desire.

gains.a: the scene gains a rule against which Kovalan's purchase can be judged, which the narrator withholds
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which no sweet word is spoken and the harm still follows, so its warning must reach the custom and the buyer, not only the woman's speech

new_concepts.gloss: dance-drama as a learned art, with its kinds, rules, gestures and accompanying music, performed before the king

source_issues: The kaathai has 179 lines as shown: 175 lines of nilaimandila akaval, matching the edition's printed last line 175, and a closing venba of 4 lines (176-179).
Lines 40, 44 and 158 carry repaired TSCII characters (ு + ட read as ூ); the repaired forms (நன்னூல், நன்குகடைப்) read correctly.
Lines 30 and 31 both read தேசிகத் திருவின் ஓசை; the repetition may be the poem's linking device or a doubled half-line, which I cannot settle.

Words are split across a space in several lines (புலமை யோனுடன் 94, ஆமந் திரிகை 142-143, ஐந்துமண் டிலத்தால் 152, வந்தவா ரம்வழி 153, நன்குகடைப் பிடித்து 158), apparently metrical division carried into the text.
